world.title: Preoperative subtalar joint stiffness predicts poor functional outcomes after supramalleolar osteotomy in an internally validated prognostic model
world.description: In this TRIPOD Type 1a study, we analyzed 108 consecutive patients who underwent computer-navigated SMO for varus ankle arthritis (2019–2024). STJ function was preoperatively stratified via a three-domain assessment (clinical range of motion, stress radiography, and CT) into Compensated (mobile, n = 88) or Decompensated (stiff, n = 20). The primary outcome was a composite of poor functional outcome (AOFAS < 80) or revision surgery. We developed a Firth-penalized logistic regression model and performed internal validation using leave-one-out cross-validation (LOOCV) and bootstrap resampling (B = 100) to estimate the optimism-corrected AUC. Multivariable Firth-penalized logistic regression identified subtalar joint (STJ) decompensation as the single independent predictor of poor outcome (OR 62.23, 95% CI 8.70–812.53, P < 0.001); preoperative talar tilt (TT) angle > 7.5° (OR 3.40, 95% CI 0.28–29.03, P = 0.293) and Takakura stage Ⅲ (OR 1.69, 95% CI 0.11–16.22, P = 0.675) did not reach significance after adjustment. The model achieved an apparent AUC of 0.957 with a LOOCV AUC of 0.880 (optimism 0.078; bootstrap optimism-corrected AUC 0.947). Calibration was adequate (LOOCV calibration slope 0.96, in-the-large − 0.06, Hosmer–Lemeshow P = 0.634). The primary outcome occurred in 90.0% (18/20) of the Decompensated group versus 2.3% (2/88) of the Compensated group (P < 0.001). A sensitivity analysis with continuous preoperative TT angle recovered a significant per-degree effect (OR 3.62, 95% CI 1.43–9.19, P = 0.007). In this preliminary, single-center cohort, preoperative STJ stiffness emerged as a potentially important independent predictor of poor functional recovery despite successful radiographic correction. The internally validated nomogram offers a preliminary risk-estimation tool that may assist preoperative counseling.
